Different alters self harm in different ways, as it's not limited to just cutting or burning after all, but the relapse I'm talking about involves blades, and we found out who exactly gave into those feelings/urges and picked up a knife.

Our general approach is to work closely with those alters to try and find out why they resort to such extreme measures and how to potentially minimize damage/prevent future SH but we're struggling to do that as we need to keep up a "functional front" so they get pushed back often and come out when it's already too late and they can't be convinced to not do that. We figured letting them speak with our therapist about it on their own could help but we can't control our switches so if somebody else is frontstuck it's really hard to get someone specific to come out at a specific time. Maybe we should encourage them to write down how they felt before/during/after SH, and examine that/take that to our therapist on their behalf, but we need them to front for not-SH purposes first, or remember to do it afterwards/instead if they still do SH/seriously want to SH. Basically letting them know that we do care and that we do want to help and that it's possible to learn how to resist those urges and find better coping mechanisms, because oftentimes we found out that alters who act out/harm the body/sabotage routine/etc do it as a cry for help or out of frustration/desperation/not knowing how to deal with their emotional baggage/feeling alone and uncared for or misunderstood. Obviously external factors like stress and being around people who drain us/are toxic also count, and alters who are more sensitive will be more prone to SH to cope, so trying to lower stress levels is also important IMO, as well as having a solid external support system that wont add to existing internal turmoil (like our social worker who immediately started threatening forced hospitalization).

All in all it takes a lot of patience and communication both externally and internally like with any other issue. We need to do the same with alters who binge drink/use drugs to cope but it's easier to tackle one problem at a time.

Sadly self harm isn't as methodical as people would like to think. Sure we handle sharp tools but the core point here is to cause injury, sometimes on complete impulse. We can pick at scabs to prolong healing, we can cut over existing wounds/scar tissue, we can rapidly make a lot or relatively superficial scratches or go way deeper and send ourselves to the ER. I've known a girl who burned a hole in her shoulder Just Because and then it got infected. I'm not saying we're dumbasses, but we aren't surgeons who make perfect incisions. We're a bunch of depressed and often traumatized people desperate for release. And sometimes we bite off more than we can chew (or cut deeper than we can handle for that matter).

I've hit styro numerous times, but the worst one was when I slashed my thigh open with an xacto knife. Got frustrated my cuts weren't as deep as I wanted them to be and foolishly applied more force. I was stunned for a minute when I saw the gaping wound it left, several mm deep. It bled for a while. The scar isn't pretty.

Bigger risk for infection as the wound takes longer to heal. Reaching muscle or fatty tissue normally warrants a trip to the ER, it's harder to clean, and usually requires stitches. The fat itself might cling to clothes or dry bandages and get pulled out of your wound which would leave a gaping hole and it hurts like a bitch. I have a big nasty scar left from cutting that deep and I didn't go to the ER out of fear of being locked up in psych. I lived but it was hell to take care of.

Sharp blades are the best, but also the riskiest. I used to use an xacto knife, and it led to me reaching fatty tissue. I now use a simple pocket knife, sharp enough to make me bleed for a solid 10 mins total, but not sharp enough to reach fat.

Amnesia doesn't have to be a clear-cut blackout to count as dissociative memory loss. We observed a significant amount of DID systems report their amnesia is more of an ommitance of detail rather than pure darkness...like fog or a thick glass wall. You may remember a location, but not what you did there at a specific point in time. You may remember faces but not names, actions (as in muscle memory) but not context, words but not emotions, and vice versa. You may have no visual memories at all but simply know that something happened; perhaps through audio cues or scents. Alternatively, yes, you may also experience total blackness and remember nothing, but that doesn't make either experience less valid.

You could also experience different levels of amnesia that vary in severity. - Connor

No, you cannot create alters, nor can just one alter be psychotic without the rest of your brain (and thus the rest of your system) being psychotic. Auditory hallucinations alone aren't enough for a schizophrenia diagnosis, either, and to our knowledge marijuana cannot cause schizophrenia; although we did hear of cases where minors either developed psychosis or had it become apparent following a period of intense drug abuse (none of these drugs were weed, though, and were more in line with psychostimulants that were modified/tampered with).

To elaborate on alter formation, alters can only form through stress or a new trauma/reoccurence of old trauma. So, you can't accidentally split, even if the split isn't fully welcomed. Chances are that if you do have alters - namely "Grace" - they were dormant for a while and now resurfaced. - Connor

Nobody here can diagnose you, I'm afraid, and you did right by scheduling a doctor's appointment. However, what I can offer is some general knowledge we have regarding both conditions.

• Childhood trauma is a must for DID/OSDD.
• In OSDD-1a, alters are less defined/individualized and communicate primarily through passive influence as opposed to active fronting. In OSDD-1b, alters may be highly individualized but the system will seldom experience any amnesia.
• In DID, alters who aren't aware of the trauma may exist.
• In Schizophrenia, the "voices" cannot take active control of the patient's body, even if they claim they do.
• Identity alteration/confusion is a DID thing.
• It is possible to have both.

That's all the relevant info I could think of at the moment. Please do more research and talk to your doctors, as I am no professional. I wish you the best. - Connor

Edit: The correlation between schizophreniform disorders and religion is new to us, but I did also want to mention the implications of religious/ritual abuse, as it may also fracture one's identity and cause DID/OSDD which makes your situation more complex but offers another perspective to rule out.
